title: 5 questions i'd ask any AI trading tool before giving it money
author: k1_r1
selftext:
disclosure: i run an SEC-registered investment adviser. not naming it, no link

feels like there's a new AI trading tool posted here every day and the comments always turn into the same argument. i spent a long time on the institutional side before any of this existed, so here's what i'd actually check before handing one my money

**1. who's legally responsible if it goes wrong?**

if a company is telling you what to buy or managing money for you, in the US they usually have to be registered as an investment adviser. you can look any of them up for free on adviserinfo.sec.gov. if it's one guy with a discord and a stripe link, the only person on the hook is you

**2. does it give the same answer twice?**

ask it the same question with the same info a few times. LLMs will happily hand you a different trade each time. if the answer changes every time you ask, the trades are going to change every time it runs too

**3. was it tested on data it never saw?**

anyone can make a strategy look great on the same data they built it on. ask if there's an out of sample period, when it starts and whether they changed anything after looking at it. if the only proof is one nice looking backtest chart i'd assume it's overfit

**4. who actually makes the trade decision, rules or the chatbot?**

if there's a written rule set you can read, you can check what it's going to do before it does it. if the chatbot is deciding on the fly there's nothing to check. ask which one it is and ask to see the rules

**5. can you look the company up?**

real name, a real person who's accountable, some history. if it's an anonymous account and a landing page that kind of answers it

the CFTC put out an advisory on this back in 2024 called "AI Won't Turn Trading Bots into Money Machines," worth a read if you've been getting DMs about bots

imo passing these is the bare minimum. i've been doing this stuff most of my career so feel free to grill me on any of it in the comments, backtesting, overfitting, whatever

comments.body: number 2 gets skipped the most. people test the strategy once and never check whether the thing picking the trades even agrees with itself.

replies.author: k1_r1
replies.body: Yes, it's a serious issue.  I think we also have a major problem with people noy DYOR.  In a space with so many low quality vibe coded tools, it takes a lot of effort to look at all the problems that could pop up.
